translations.title: Data Representations
translations.explanation: Data Representations is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “One-variable Statistics”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:HSS-ID.A.1. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Represent data with plots on the real number line (dot plots, histograms, and box plots). Instructional focus: Students summarize, display, compare, and model data while connecting statistics to the context and variability. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Data Representations. Choose displays and statistics that fit the data type. Describe center, spread, shape, and unusual values. In bivariate data, association does not by itself establish causation.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: For the data [9, 11, 13, 13, 15], the mean is (9 + 11 + 13 + 13 + 15)/5 = 12.2. The range is 15 - 9 = 6. Example 2: For the data [8, 10, 12, 12, 14], the mean is (8 + 10 + 12 + 12 + 14)/5 = 11.2. The range is 14 - 8 = 6.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: verify there are 5 observations. Step 2: add them to obtain 61. Step 3: divide by 5 to get mean 12.2. Step 4: subtract minimum 9 from maximum 15 to get range 6 and interpret both statistics in context. Step 1: verify there are 5 observations. Step 2: add them to obtain 56. Step 3: divide by 5 to get mean 11.2. Step 4: subtract minimum 8 from maximum 14 to get range 6 and interpret both statistics in context.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Data Representations. Do not hide scale or outliers that materially change interpretation. Do not use a regression equation outside the meaningful domain without justification.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Data Representations. Represent the data appropriately, calculate or interpret the relevant statistic or model, describe variability, and state a contextual conclusion.

Krok 4: odejmij minimum 9 od maksimum 15 i otrzymaj rozstęp 6. Krok 1: sprawdź, że jest 5 obserwacji. Krok 2: suma wynosi 56. Krok 3: podziel przez 5 i otrzymaj średnią 11.2. translations.title: Planning a Pizza Party

It is aligned exactly to CCSS:HSA-CED.A.2, CCSS:HSA-CED.A.3, CCSS:HSN-Q.A.2. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Create equations in two or more variables to represent relationships between quantities; graph equations on coordinate axes with labels and scales. Represent constraints by equations or inequalities, and by systems of equations and/or inequalities, and interpret solutions as viable or non-viable options in a modeling context. For example, represent inequalities describing nutritional and cost constraints on combinations of different foods. Define appropriate quantities for the purpose of descriptive modeling. Instructional focus: Students define variables and create equations or inequalities that model relationships among quantities. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Planning a Pizza Party. Define each variable with units, translate each relationship before solving, and keep the equation dimensionally and contextually consistent. Rearranging a formula must use equivalent operations.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: A situation has fixed amount 17 and increases by 5 per unit. Model it by y=5x+17. At x=7, y=52. Example 2: A situation has fixed amount 11 and increases by 8 per unit. Model it by y=8x+11. At x=2, y=27.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: define x as number of units and y as total. Step 2: variable part is 5x. Step 3: add fixed amount 17. Step 4: substitute x=7: y=5(7)+17=52. Step 1: define x as number of units and y as total. Step 2: variable part is 8x. Step 3: add fixed amount 11. Step 4: substitute x=2: y=8(2)+11=27.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Planning a Pizza Party. Do not start manipulating symbols before stating what they mean. Avoid mixing total quantities with rates or per-unit quantities without the correct factor.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Planning a Pizza Party. Define variables, translate the relationship, form an equation or inequality, and check that the model and units match the situation.

translations.title: Writing Equations to Model Relationships (Part 1)
translations.explanation: Writing Equations to Model Relationships (Part 1) is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Linear Equations, Inequalities, and Systems”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:HSA-CED.A.2, CCSS:HSA-CED.A.3. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Create equations in two or more variables to represent relationships between quantities; graph equations on coordinate axes with labels and scales. Represent constraints by equations or inequalities, and by systems of equations and/or inequalities, and interpret solutions as viable or non-viable options in a modeling context. For example, represent inequalities describing nutritional and cost constraints on combinations of different foods. Instructional focus: Students define variables and create equations or inequalities that model relationships among quantities. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Writing Equations to Model Relationships (Part 1). Define each variable with units, translate each relationship before solving, and keep the equation dimensionally and contextually consistent. Rearranging a formula must use equivalent operations.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: A situation has fixed amount 7 and increases by 4 per unit. Model it by y=4x+7. At x=7, y=35. Example 2: A situation has fixed amount 28 and increases by 11 per unit. Model it by y=11x+28. At x=3, y=61.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: define x as number of units and y as total. Step 2: variable part is 4x. Step 3: add fixed amount 7. Step 4: substitute x=7: y=4(7)+7=35. Step 1: define x as number of units and y as total. Step 2: variable part is 11x. Step 3: add fixed amount 28. Step 4: substitute x=3: y=11(3)+28=61.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Writing Equations to Model Relationships (Part 1). Do not start manipulating symbols before stating what they mean. Avoid mixing total quantities with rates or per-unit quantities without the correct factor.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Writing Equations to Model Relationships (Part 1). Define variables, translate the relationship, form an equation or inequality, and check that the model and units match the situation.

translations.title: Equations and Their Solutions
translations.explanation: Equations and Their Solutions is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Linear Equations, Inequalities, and Systems”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:HSA-REI.B.3. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Solve linear equations and inequalities in one variable, including equations with coefficients represented by letters. Instructional focus: Students solve equations, inequalities, and systems by using equivalent reasoning and interpreting solutions as values or intersection points. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Equations and Their Solutions. Apply the same equivalence-preserving operation to both sides. For inequalities, multiplying or dividing by a negative reverses the inequality sign. A solution to a system must satisfy every equation in the system.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Solve the system x+y=10 and x-y=-4. Adding equations gives 2x=6, so x=3; then y=7. Example 2: Solve the system x+y=9 and x-y=1. Adding equations gives 2x=10, so x=5; then y=4.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: add the equations to eliminate y: 2x=6. Step 2: divide by 2 to get x=3. Step 3: substitute into x+y=10: 3+y=10, so y=7. Step 4: verify both original equations. Step 1: add the equations to eliminate y: 2x=10. Step 2: divide by 2 to get x=5. Step 3: substitute into x+y=9: 5+y=9, so y=4. Step 4: verify both original equations.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Equations and Their Solutions. Do not accept an extraneous solution created by squaring, clearing denominators, or other non-reversible steps. Verify solutions in the original relation.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Equations and Their Solutions. Transform consistently, solve, and substitute the candidate solution back into the original equation, inequality, or system.

translations.workedExamples: Przykład 1: Rozwiąż układ x+y=10 oraz x-y=-4. Po dodaniu równań: 2x=6, więc x=3; następnie y=7. Przykład 2: Rozwiąż układ x+y=9 oraz x-y=1. Po dodaniu równań: 2x=10, więc x=5; następnie y=4.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Krok 1: dodaj równania i wyeliminuj y: 2x=6. Krok 2: podziel przez 2: x=3. Krok 3: podstaw do x+y=10: y=7. Krok 4: sprawdź oba równania wyjściowe. Krok 1: dodaj równania i wyeliminuj y: 2x=10. Krok 2: podziel przez 2: x=5. Krok 3: podstaw do x+y=9: y=4. Krok 4: sprawdź oba równania wyjściowe.
translations.commonMistakes: Cel tej lekcji: Równania and Their Solutions. Nie przyjmuj rozwiązania pozornego powstałego np. przy podnoszeniu do kwadratu lub usuwaniu mianowników. Sprawdzaj rozwiązania w relacji wyjściowej.

translations.title: Systems of Linear Equations and Their Solutions
translations.explanation: Systems of Linear Equations and Their Solutions is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Linear Equations, Inequalities, and Systems”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:HSA-CED.A.3, CCSS:HSA-REI.C.6. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Represent constraints by equations or inequalities, and by systems of equations and/or inequalities, and interpret solutions as viable or non-viable options in a modeling context. For example, represent inequalities describing nutritional and cost constraints on combinations of different foods. Solve systems of linear equations exactly and approximately (e.g., with graphs), focusing on pairs of linear equations in two variables. Instructional focus: Students define variables and create equations or inequalities that model relationships among quantities. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Systems of Linear Equations and Their Solutions. Define each variable with units, translate each relationship before solving, and keep the equation dimensionally and contextually consistent. Rearranging a formula must use equivalent operations.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: A situation has fixed amount 17 and increases by 6 per unit. Model it by y=6x+17. At x=4, y=41. Example 2: A situation has fixed amount 25 and increases by 12 per unit. Model it by y=12x+25. At x=8, y=121.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: define x as number of units and y as total. Step 2: variable part is 6x. Step 3: add fixed amount 17. Step 4: substitute x=4: y=6(4)+17=41. Step 1: define x as number of units and y as total. Step 2: variable part is 12x. Step 3: add fixed amount 25. Step 4: substitute x=8: y=12(8)+25=121.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Systems of Linear Equations and Their Solutions. Do not start manipulating symbols before stating what they mean. Avoid mixing total quantities with rates or per-unit quantities without the correct factor.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Systems of Linear Equations and Their Solutions. Define variables, translate the relationship, form an equation or inequality, and check that the model and units match the situation.

translations.title: Solving Problems with Systems of Linear Inequalities in Two Variables

It is aligned exactly to CCSS:HSA-REI.D.12. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Graph the solutions to a linear inequality in two variables as a half-plane (excluding the boundary in the case of a strict inequality), and graph the solution set to a system of linear inequalities in two variables as the intersection of the corresponding half-planes. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Solving Problems with Systems of Linear Inequalities in Two Variables. Apply the same equivalence-preserving operation to both sides. For inequalities, multiplying or dividing by a negative reverses the inequality sign. A solution to a system must satisfy every equation in the system.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Solve the system x+y=8 and x-y=6. Adding equations gives 2x=14, so x=7; then y=1. Example 2: Solve the system x+y=5 and x-y=-3. Adding equations gives 2x=2, so x=1; then y=4.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: add the equations to eliminate y: 2x=14. Step 2: divide by 2 to get x=7. Step 3: substitute into x+y=8: 7+y=8, so y=1. Step 4: verify both original equations. Step 1: add the equations to eliminate y: 2x=2. Step 2: divide by 2 to get x=1. Step 3: substitute into x+y=5: 1+y=5, so y=4. Step 4: verify both original equations.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Solving Problems with Systems of Linear Inequalities in Two Variables. Do not accept an extraneous solution created by squaring, clearing denominators, or other non-reversible steps. Verify solutions in the original relation.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Solving Problems with Systems of Linear Inequalities in Two Variables. Transform consistently, solve, and substitute the candidate solution back into the original equation, inequality, or system.

translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Residuals. Carry units through calculations, convert by multiplying by a form of 1, choose a sensible level of precision, and define variables with units before building a model.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Convert 4 km to meters. Since 1 km = 1000 m, 4 km × (1000 m / 1 km) = 4000 m. Example 2: Convert 12 km to meters. Since 1 km = 1000 m, 12 km × (1000 m / 1 km) = 12000 m.

Step 1: write 12 km. Step 2: multiply by the conversion factor 1000 m / 1 km. Step 3: cancel km. Step 4: calculate 12×1000=12000; the result is 12000 m.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Residuals. Do not cancel units that are not factors. Do not report more precision than the measurements justify. Check dimensional consistency before trusting a formula.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Residuals. Define the quantities and units, convert consistently, calculate, and interpret the numerical value with appropriate precision.

The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Represent data on two quantitative variables on a scatter plot, and describe how the variables are related. a. Fit a function to the data; use functions fitted to data to solve problems in the context of the data. Use given functions or choose a function suggested by the context. Emphasize linear, quadratic, and exponential models. b. Informally assess the fit of a function by plotting and analyzing residuals. c. Fit a linear function for a scatter plot that suggests a linear association. Interpret the slope (rate of change) and the intercept (constant term) of a linear model in the context of the data. Compute (using technology) and interpret the correlation coefficient of a linear fit. Distinguish between correlation and causation. Instructional focus: Students summarize, display, compare, and model data while connecting statistics to the context and variability. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Fossils and Flags. Choose displays and statistics that fit the data type. Describe center, spread, shape, and unusual values. In bivariate data, association does not by itself establish causation.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: For the data [8, 10, 12, 12, 14], the mean is (8 + 10 + 12 + 12 + 14)/5 = 11.2. The range is 14 - 8 = 6. Example 2: For the data [4, 6, 8, 8, 10], the mean is (4 + 6 + 8 + 8 + 10)/5 = 7.2. The range is 10 - 4 = 6.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: verify there are 5 observations. Step 2: add them to obtain 56. Step 3: divide by 5 to get mean 11.2. Step 4: subtract minimum 8 from maximum 14 to get range 6 and interpret both statistics in context. Step 1: verify there are 5 observations. Step 2: add them to obtain 36. Step 3: divide by 5 to get mean 7.2. Step 4: subtract minimum 4 from maximum 10 to get range 6 and interpret both statistics in context.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Fossils and Flags. Do not hide scale or outliers that materially change interpretation. Do not use a regression equation outside the meaningful domain without justification.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Fossils and Flags. Represent the data appropriately, calculate or interpret the relevant statistic or model, describe variability, and state a contextual conclusion.

translations.title: Describing and Graphing Situations
translations.explanation: Describing and Graphing Situations is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Functions”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:HSF-IF.A.1, CCSS:HSF-IF.B.4. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Understand that a function from one set (called the domain) to another set (called the range) assigns to each element of the domain exactly one element of the range. If f is a function and x is an element of its domain, then f(x) denotes the output of f corresponding to the input x. The graph of f is the graph of the equation y = f(x). For a function that models a relationship between two quantities, interpret key features of graphs and tables in terms of the quantities, and sketch graphs showing key features given a verbal description of the relationship. Key features include: intercepts; intervals where the function is increasing, decreasing, positive, or negat ive; relative maximums and minimums; symmetries; end behavior; and periodicity .★ Instructional focus: Students interpret function notation, domain, range, rates of change, graph features, and multiple representations in context. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Describing and Graphing Situations. f(x) denotes the output corresponding to input x. Domain restrictions come from the context or formula. Intercepts, intervals of increase/decrease, maxima/minima, and average rate of change describe different features.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: For f(x) = 5x + 2, f(4) = 5(4) + 2 = 22. The rate of change is 5 and the output at x=0 is 2. Example 2: For f(x) = 3x + 7, f(3) = 3(3) + 7 = 16. The rate of change is 3 and the output at x=0 is 7.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify input x=4. Step 2: substitute into f(x)=5x+2. Step 3: multiply 5×4=20. Step 4: add 2 to obtain 22. Step 5: interpret slope 5 and initial value 2 with the problem units. Step 1: identify input x=3. Step 2: substitute into f(x)=3x+7. Step 3: multiply 3×3=9. Step 4: add 7 to obtain 16. Step 5: interpret slope 3 and initial value 7 with the problem units.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Describing and Graphing Situations. Do not read a graph without checking scale and units. Do not confuse f(x) with multiplication f·x. Distinguish an average rate over an interval from an instantaneous or point value.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Describing and Graphing Situations. Identify the representation and domain, calculate or read the requested feature, and interpret it with the input and output units.

translations.title: Absolute Value Functions (Part 2)
translations.explanation: Absolute Value Functions (Part 2) is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Functions”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:HSF-BF.A.1, CCSS:HSF-BF.B.3, CCSS:HSF-IF.C.7. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Write a function that describes a relationship between two quantities.★ a. Determine an explicit expression, a recursive process, or steps for calculation from a context. b. Combine standard function types using arithmetic operations. For example, build a function that models the temperature of a cooling body by adding a constant function to a decaying exponential, and relate these functions to the model. c. (+) Compose functions. For example, if T(y) is the temperature in the atmosphere as a function of height, and h(t) is the height of a weather balloon as a function of time, then T(h(t)) is the temperature at the location of the weather balloon as a function of time. Identify the effect on the graph of replacing f(x) by f(x) + k, k f(x), f(kx), and f(x + k) for specific values of k (both positive and negative); find the value of k given the graphs. Experiment with cases and illustrate an explanation of the effects on the graph using technology. Include recognizing even and odd functions from their graphs and algebraic expressions for them. Graph functions expressed symbolically and show key features of the graph, by hand in simple cases and using technology for more complicated cases.★ a. Graph linear and quadratic functions and show intercepts, maxima, and minima. b. Graph square root, cube root, and piecewise-defined functions, including step functions and absolute valu... Instructional focus: Students build new functions from relationships, sequences, transformations, compositions, and inverse processes. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Absolute Value Functions (Part 2). Choose a function family that matches the relationship. Transformations change inputs or outputs in predictable ways. Composition substitutes one function into another; an inverse reverses the original mapping on an appropriate domain.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Let f(x)=5x+4. For x=3, f(3)=19. Solving y=5x+4 for x gives f⁻¹(y)=(y-4)/5; thus f⁻¹(19)=3. Example 2: Let f(x)=2x+3. For x=4, f(4)=11. Solving y=2x+3 for x gives f⁻¹(y)=(y-3)/2; thus f⁻¹(11)=4.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: evaluate f(3)=5(3)+4=19. Step 2: write y=5x+4. Step 3: subtract 4 and divide by 5: x=(y-4)/5. Step 4: substitute y=19 to recover x=3. Step 1: evaluate f(4)=2(4)+3=11. Step 2: write y=2x+3. Step 3: subtract 3 and divide by 2: x=(y-3)/2. Step 4: substitute y=11 to recover x=4.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Absolute Value Functions (Part 2). Do not assume every function has an inverse function on its full domain. Track whether a transformation acts inside or outside the function.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Absolute Value Functions (Part 2). Build the rule from the relationship, state its domain, apply transformations or composition carefully, and verify with input-output pairs.

translations.title: Growing and Growing
translations.explanation: Growing and Growing is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Introduction to Exponential Functions”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:HSF-IF.B.4, CCSS:HSF-LE.A.3. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: For a function that models a relationship between two quantities, interpret key features of graphs and tables in terms of the quantities, and sketch graphs showing key features given a verbal description of the relationship. Key features include: intercepts; intervals where the function is increasing, decreasing, positive, or negat ive; relative maximums and minimums; symmetries; end behavior; and periodicity .★ Observe using graphs and tables that a quantity increasing exponentially eventually exceeds a quantity increasing linearly, quadratically, or (more generally) as a polynomial function. Instructional focus: Students interpret function notation, domain, range, rates of change, graph features, and multiple representations in context. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Growing and Growing. f(x) denotes the output corresponding to input x. Domain restrictions come from the context or formula. Intercepts, intervals of increase/decrease, maxima/minima, and average rate of change describe different features.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: For f(x) = 5x + 2, f(3) = 5(3) + 2 = 17. The rate of change is 5 and the output at x=0 is 2. Example 2: For f(x) = 5x + 6, f(4) = 5(4) + 6 = 26. The rate of change is 5 and the output at x=0 is 6.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify input x=3. Step 2: substitute into f(x)=5x+2. Step 3: multiply 5×3=15. Step 4: add 2 to obtain 17. Step 5: interpret slope 5 and initial value 2 with the problem units. Step 1: identify input x=4. Step 2: substitute into f(x)=5x+6. Step 3: multiply 5×4=20. Step 4: add 6 to obtain 26. Step 5: interpret slope 5 and initial value 6 with the problem units.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Growing and Growing. Do not read a graph without checking scale and units. Do not confuse f(x) with multiplication f·x. Distinguish an average rate over an interval from an instantaneous or point value.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Growing and Growing. Identify the representation and domain, calculate or read the requested feature, and interpret it with the input and output units.

translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Compounding Interest. Choose a function family that matches the relationship. Transformations change inputs or outputs in predictable ways. Composition substitutes one function into another; an inverse reverses the original mapping on an appropriate domain.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Let f(x)=4x+4. For x=5, f(5)=24. Solving y=4x+4 for x gives f⁻¹(y)=(y-4)/4; thus f⁻¹(24)=5. Example 2: Let f(x)=3x+1. For x=1, f(1)=4. Solving y=3x+1 for x gives f⁻¹(y)=(y-1)/3; thus f⁻¹(4)=1.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: evaluate f(5)=4(5)+4=24. Step 2: write y=4x+4. Step 3: subtract 4 and divide by 4: x=(y-4)/4. Step 4: substitute y=24 to recover x=5. Step 1: evaluate f(1)=3(1)+1=4. Step 2: write y=3x+1. Step 3: subtract 1 and divide by 3: x=(y-1)/3. Step 4: substitute y=4 to recover x=1.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Compounding Interest. Do not assume every function has an inverse function on its full domain. Track whether a transformation acts inside or outside the function.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Compounding Interest. Build the rule from the relationship, state its domain, apply transformations or composition carefully, and verify with input-output pairs.

translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Starting at 46, growth of 11% per period is modeled by y=46(1.11)^t. translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Changes over Equal Intervals. Do not decide the model type from one data pair. A percent increase is multiplicative, not a fixed additive amount. Check whether the factor is greater than or between 0 and 1.

translations.title: A Different Kind of Change
translations.explanation: A Different Kind of Change is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Introduction to Quadratic Functions”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:HSF-BF.A.1. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Write a function that describes a relationship between two quantities.★ a. Determine an explicit expression, a recursive process, or steps for calculation from a context. b. Combine standard function types using arithmetic operations. For example, build a function that models the temperature of a cooling body by adding a constant function to a decaying exponential, and relate these functions to the model. c. (+) Compose functions. For example, if T(y) is the temperature in the atmosphere as a function of height, and h(t) is the height of a weather balloon as a function of time, then T(h(t)) is the temperature at the location of the weather balloon as a function of time. Instructional focus: Students build new functions from relationships, sequences, transformations, compositions, and inverse processes. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: A Different Kind of Change. Choose a function family that matches the relationship. Transformations change inputs or outputs in predictable ways. Composition substitutes one function into another; an inverse reverses the original mapping on an appropriate domain.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Let f(x)=2x+5. For x=4, f(4)=13. Solving y=2x+5 for x gives f⁻¹(y)=(y-5)/2; thus f⁻¹(13)=4. Example 2: Let f(x)=4x+6. For x=3, f(3)=18. Solving y=4x+6 for x gives f⁻¹(y)=(y-6)/4; thus f⁻¹(18)=3.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: evaluate f(4)=2(4)+5=13. Step 2: write y=2x+5. Step 3: subtract 5 and divide by 2: x=(y-5)/2. Step 4: substitute y=13 to recover x=4. Step 1: evaluate f(3)=4(3)+6=18. Step 2: write y=4x+6. Step 3: subtract 6 and divide by 4: x=(y-6)/4. Step 4: substitute y=18 to recover x=3.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: A Different Kind of Change. Do not assume every function has an inverse function on its full domain. Track whether a transformation acts inside or outside the function.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: A Different Kind of Change. Build the rule from the relationship, state its domain, apply transformations or composition carefully, and verify with input-output pairs.

translations.title: When and Why Do We Write Quadratic Equations?
translations.explanation: When and Why Do We Write Quadratic Equations? is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Quadratic Equations”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:HSA-REI.B.4. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Solve quadratic equations in one variable. a. Use the method of completing the square to transform any quadratic equation in x into an equation of the form (x – p)2 = q that has the same solutions. Derive the quadratic formula from this form. b. Solve quadratic equations by inspection (e.g., for x2 = 49), taking square roots, completing the square, the quadratic formula and factoring, as appropriate to the initial form of the equation. Recognize when the quadratic formula gives complex solutions and write them as a ± bi f or real numbers a and b. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: When and Why Do We Write Quadratic Equations?. Apply the same equivalence-preserving operation to both sides. For inequalities, multiplying or dividing by a negative reverses the inequality sign. A solution to a system must satisfy every equation in the system.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Solve the system x+y=9 and x-y=5. Adding equations gives 2x=14, so x=7; then y=2. Example 2: Solve the system x+y=13 and x-y=-1. Adding equations gives 2x=12, so x=6; then y=7.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: add the equations to eliminate y: 2x=14. Step 2: divide by 2 to get x=7. Step 3: substitute into x+y=9: 7+y=9, so y=2. Step 4: verify both original equations. Step 1: add the equations to eliminate y: 2x=12. Step 2: divide by 2 to get x=6. Step 3: substitute into x+y=13: 6+y=13, so y=7. Step 4: verify both original equations.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: When and Why Do We Write Quadratic Equations?. Do not accept an extraneous solution created by squaring, clearing denominators, or other non-reversible steps. Verify solutions in the original relation.

translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Rewriting Quadratic Expressions in Factored Form (Part 1). Equivalent forms can reveal different features. translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Expand (x+5)(x+1) to get x²+6x+5; therefore x²+6x+5 factors back to (x+5)(x+1). Example 2: Expand (x+4)(x+1) to get x²+5x+4; therefore x²+5x+4 factors back to (x+4)(x+1).
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: multiply x·x=x². Step 2: outer and inner terms give 1x+5x=6x. Step 3: constants give 5×1=5. Step 4: combine as x²+6x+5 and verify the factorization by re-expanding. Step 1: multiply x·x=x². Step 2: outer and inner terms give 1x+4x=5x. Step 3: constants give 4×1=4. Step 4: combine as x²+5x+4 and verify the factorization by re-expanding.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Rewriting Quadratic Expressions in Factored Form (Part 1). Do not combine unlike terms or cancel across addition. Check a transformed expression by expansion or substitution.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Rewriting Quadratic Expressions in Factored Form (Part 1). Identify the useful structure, apply an equivalence-preserving transformation, and check the new form against the original.

translations.title: Solving Quadratic Equations by Using Factored Form
translations.explanation: Solving Quadratic Equations by Using Factored Form is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Quadratic Equations”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:HSA-REI.B.4, CCSS:HSA-SSE.B.3. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Solve quadratic equations in one variable. a. Use the method of completing the square to transform any quadratic equation in x into an equation of the form (x – p)2 = q that has the same solutions. Derive the quadratic formula from this form. b. Solve quadratic equations by inspection (e.g., for x2 = 49), taking square roots, completing the square, the quadratic formula and factoring, as appropriate to the initial form of the equation. Recognize when the quadratic formula gives complex solutions and write them as a ± bi f or real numbers a and b. Choose and produce an equivalent form of an expression to reveal and explain properties of the quantity represented by the expression.★ a. Factor a quadratic expression to reveal the zeros of the function it defines. b. Complete the square in a quadratic expression to reveal the maximum or minimum value of the function it defines. c. Use the properties of exponents to transform expressions for exponential functions. For example the expression 1.15t can be rewritten as (1.151/12)12t ≈ 1.01212t to reveal the approximate equivalent monthly interest rate if the annual rate is 15%. Instructional focus: Students solve equations, inequalities, and systems by using equivalent reasoning and interpreting solutions as values or intersection points. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Solving Quadratic Equations by Using Factored Form. Apply the same equivalence-preserving operation to both sides. For inequalities, multiplying or dividing by a negative reverses the inequality sign. A solution to a system must satisfy every equation in the system.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Solve the system x+y=9 and x-y=-1. Adding equations gives 2x=8, so x=4; then y=5. Example 2: Solve the system x+y=13 and x-y=-1. Adding equations gives 2x=12, so x=6; then y=7.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: add the equations to eliminate y: 2x=8. Step 2: divide by 2 to get x=4. Step 3: substitute into x+y=9: 4+y=9, so y=5. Step 4: verify both original equations. Step 1: add the equations to eliminate y: 2x=12. Step 2: divide by 2 to get x=6. Step 3: substitute into x+y=13: 6+y=13, so y=7. Step 4: verify both original equations.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Solving Quadratic Equations by Using Factored Form. Do not accept an extraneous solution created by squaring, clearing denominators, or other non-reversible steps. Verify solutions in the original relation.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Solving Quadratic Equations by Using Factored Form. Transform consistently, solve, and substitute the candidate solution back into the original equation, inequality, or system.

For example the expression 1.15t can be rewritten as (1.151/12)12t ≈ 1.01212t to reveal the approximate equivalent monthly interest rate if the annual rate is 15%. For example, given a graph of one quadratic function and an algebraic expression for another, say which has the larger maximum. translations.title: Using Quadratic Equations to Model Situations and Solve Problems
translations.explanation: Using Quadratic Equations to Model Situations and Solve Problems is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Quadratic Equations”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:HSA-REI.B.4, CCSS:HSA-REI.C.7, CCSS:HSF-IF.C.8. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Solve quadratic equations in one variable. a. Use the method of completing the square to transform any quadratic equation in x into an equation of the form (x – p)2 = q that has the same solutions. Derive the quadratic formula from this form. b. Solve quadratic equations by inspection (e.g., for x2 = 49), taking square roots, completing the square, the quadratic formula and factoring, as appropriate to the initial form of the equation. Recognize when the quadratic formula gives complex solutions and write them as a ± bi f or real numbers a and b. Solve a simple system consisting of a linear equation and a quadratic equation in two variables algebraically and graphically. For example, find the points of intersection between the line y = –3x and the circle x2 + y2 = 3. Write a function defined by an expression in different but equivalent forms to reveal and explain different properties of the function. a. Use the process of factoring and completing the square in a quadratic function to show zeros, extreme values, and symmetry of the graph, and interpret these in terms of a context. b. Use the properties of exponents to interpret expressions for exponential functions. For example, identify percent rate of change in functions such as y = (1.02)t, y = (0.97)t, y = (1.01)12t, y = (1.2)t/10, and classify them as representing exponential growth or decay. Instructional focus: Students solve equations, inequalities, and systems by using equivalent reasoning and interpreting solutions as values or intersection points. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Using Quadratic Equations to Model Situations and Solve Problems. Apply the same equivalence-preserving operation to both sides. For inequalities, multiplying or dividing by a negative reverses the inequality sign. A solution to a system must satisfy every equation in the system.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Solve the system x+y=8 and x-y=-2. Adding equations gives 2x=6, so x=3; then y=5. Example 2: Solve the system x+y=10 and x-y=-2. Adding equations gives 2x=8, so x=4; then y=6.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: add the equations to eliminate y: 2x=6. Step 2: divide by 2 to get x=3. Step 3: substitute into x+y=8: 3+y=8, so y=5. Step 4: verify both original equations. Step 1: add the equations to eliminate y: 2x=8. Step 2: divide by 2 to get x=4. Step 3: substitute into x+y=10: 4+y=10, so y=6. Step 4: verify both original equations.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Using Quadratic Equations to Model Situations and Solve Problems. Do not accept an extraneous solution created by squaring, clearing denominators, or other non-reversible steps. Verify solutions in the original relation.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Using Quadratic Equations to Model Situations and Solve Problems. Transform consistently, solve, and substitute the candidate solution back into the original equation, inequality, or system.

translations.title: Using Kwadratowe Równania to Model Situations and Rozwiązywanie Problems
translations.explanation: Lekcja „Using Kwadratowe Równania to Model Situations and Rozwiązywanie Problems” należy do działu „Quadratic Equations” i jest dokładnie powiązana ze standardami CCSS:HSA-REI.B.4, CCSS:HSA-REI.C.7, CCSS:HSF-IF.C.8. Główny kierunek pracy: Uczeń rozwiązuje równania, nierówności i układy przez przekształcenia równoważne oraz interpretuje rozwiązania jako wartości lub punkty przecięcia. Tytuł i kolejność pochodzą z zaakceptowanego źródła pedagogicznego, natomiast granice merytoryczne wyznaczają oficjalne standardy Common Core.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Cel tej lekcji: Using Kwadratowe Równania to Model Situations and Rozwiązywanie Problems. Wykonuj to samo działanie zachowujące równoważność po obu stronach. W nierówności mnożenie lub dzielenie przez liczbę ujemną odwraca znak. Rozwiązanie układu musi spełniać każde równanie.
translations.workedExamples: Przykład 1: Rozwiąż układ x+y=8 oraz x-y=-2. Po dodaniu równań: 2x=6, więc x=3; następnie y=5. Przykład 2: Rozwiąż układ x+y=10 oraz x-y=-2. Po dodaniu równań: 2x=8, więc x=4; następnie y=6.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Krok 1: dodaj równania i wyeliminuj y: 2x=6. Krok 2: podziel przez 2: x=3. Krok 3: podstaw do x+y=8: y=5. Krok 4: sprawdź oba równania wyjściowe. Krok 1: dodaj równania i wyeliminuj y: 2x=8. Krok 2: podziel przez 2: x=4. Krok 3: podstaw do x+y=10: y=6. Krok 4: sprawdź oba równania wyjściowe.
translations.commonMistakes: Cel tej lekcji: Using Kwadratowe Równania to Model Situations and Rozwiązywanie Problems. Nie przyjmuj rozwiązania pozornego powstałego np. przy podnoszeniu do kwadratu lub usuwaniu mianowników. Sprawdzaj rozwiązania w relacji wyjściowej.
translations.quickSummary: Cel tej lekcji: Using Kwadratowe Równania to Model Situations and Rozwiązywanie Problems. Przekształcaj konsekwentnie, rozwiąż i podstaw otrzymaną wartość do pierwotnego równania, nierówności lub układu.
